name: Radish
label: radish strip

planting.note: four 8 ft rows, sown 1 in apart, thinned to 1 in

bed30.note: four rows 6 in apart, thinned to 1 in — sown thick, pulled fast

watch_for: flea beetles and cabbage root maggot — row cover at seeding keeps both out (NEVMG); hot, dry spells make roots pithy and pungent
watering: Keep evenly moist; a dry spell mid-growth makes roots hot and pithy.
method_notes: The fastest crop in the garden — NEVMG: 21–28 days, sow every ~10 days as a rotation, spring and fall only (summer heat ruins quality). Scatter a few seeds in slow-germinating carrot, beet and parsnip rows to mark them, a UMaine-published practice. No storage worth planning: pull as they size up.
source: New England Vegetable Management Guide (UMass/UNH/UVM/UMaine): Radish crop + insect control pages (21–28 days, 10-day interval, row cover for flea beetles/root maggot); UMaine Cooperative Extension Maine Home Garden News April 2015 (row-marker practice); UMaine Bulletins #2190 (varieties) and Planting Chart for the Home Vegetable Garden (Lois Stack).

name: Turnip
label: turnip bed

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 4–6 in

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart, thinned to 6 in — turnips hate crowding

watch_for: flea beetles on seedlings (a mid-July sowing skips the worst spring flush), cabbage root maggot, clubroot in brassica rotation
watering: Even moisture; drought turns roots woody and bitter.
method_notes: Fast and forgiving: spring crop as soon as ground is workable, plus a midsummer sowing for fall. Frost sweetens them, but MOFGA is explicit that turnips cannot withstand freezing — lift before hard freeze. Best pulled at 2–4 in; larger roots get fibrous. Greens are a harvest in their own right.
source: MOFGA 'Grow Turnips' (R. Bailey, 2004, Maine); UMaine Cooperative Extension Planting Chart (Lois Stack) — seed 1/4–1/2 in deep, rows 12–18 in; NEVMG Rutabaga and Turnip Insect Control; UMaine Bulletin #2190 (varieties: Hakurei, Purple Top White Globe, Tokyo Cross); UNH Extension Planting & Maturity Dates of Vegetables in NH.

name: Rutabaga
label: rutabaga bed

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 6–8 in

bed30.note: two rows 12 in apart, thinned to 8 in for full-size roots

watch_for: flea beetles on young plants (the reason Maine sows mid-June, after the first flush), cabbage root maggot, clubroot in brassica rotation
watering: Deep taproot tolerates mild drought; water through late-summer dry spells while roots bulk.
method_notes: The Maine fall storage root: sow mid-June per MOFGA to dodge flea beetles, harvest early October before the ground freezes — rutabagas withstand some freezing but are dug and stored near 32–38°F, not left in. Single sowing, no succession. One of the Coleman winter-table crops from storage, not from the bed.
source: MOFGA 'Grow Turnips' (R. Bailey, 2004, Maine — 90–100 days, mid-June sowing, thin 6–8 in, store 32–38°F); NEVMG Rutabaga and Turnip Insect Control; Fedco Seeds (Laurentian); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (varieties: American Purple Top, Joan, Laurentian, York); UNH Extension Planting & Maturity Dates.

name: Parsnip
label: parsnip rows

planting.note: two 8 ft rows, seed 1 in apart, thin to 3 in

bed30.note: three rows 9 in apart, thinned to 3 in; deep, stone-free soil or roots fork

watch_for: carrot rust fly — NEVMG notes it also attacks parsnips, mining the upper root; canker and forking in heavy or manured soil; parsnip seed barely keeps a year, sow fresh
watering: Even, deep moisture all season; dry spells produce tough, cracked roots.
method_notes: The classic in-ground winter root: UMaine Bulletin #4311 and Coleman's winter-harvest practice both leave parsnips to overwinter under mulch for sweeter spring roots (frost converts starch to sugar). Sow mid-to-late April in coastal Maine (UMaine planting chart; coastal dates run 10–14 days earlier than central). Single sowing. NOTE: NEVMG flags that over-wintered crops can harbor carrot rust fly larvae — weigh the trade and rotate beds.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension Bulletin #4311 (overwintering for a sweeter spring product); UMaine Planting Chart (Lois Stack) — rows 18–24 in, thin 2–4 in; NEVMG Carrot and Parsnip Insect Control (rust fly on parsnips, onion intercropping); Fedco Seeds (Harris Model, 120 days from direct seeding); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (Harris Model, Lancer).

name: Celeriac
label: celeriac row

planting.note: two 8 ft rows 12 in apart, plants 6–8 in apart

bed30.note: double rows 14 in apart, plants 6 in apart — UMaine Highmoor trials found 6 in yields most per bed-foot

watch_for: leaf blight (Septoria) in humid spells, leafminers, aphids; black heart and cracked roots from uneven moisture — celery relatives need steady water
watering: Consistent moisture all season; uneven watering cracks the root and brings black heart.
method_notes: Slow, cool-season, worth it: start indoors ~10 weeks before last frost (UMaine seeded 13 Apr for a 22 Jun transplant), set out after frost, dig September–November before hard freeze — it is dug and stored, not a true winter-harvest root. UMaine Highmoor 2022 trial: 6 in in-row on double rows 14 in apart gave the greatest marketable yield per bed-foot (cultivars Brilliant, Balena best); 100+ days from transplant to mature. Stores 6–8 months near freezing — the winter stand-in for celery flavor.
source: UMaine Cooperative Extension Highmoor Farm Celeriac Evaluation 2022 (Ginakes, Hutton, Handley — spacing trial, 121 days to harvest); MOFGA 'Celeriac' (100 days from transplant, 6–8 in spacing, 3–5 in harvest, storage); Johnny's Selected Seeds (Brilliant, 100 days from transplant); UMaine Bulletin #2190 (celery varieties Utah 52-70, Ventura).

name: Sweet potato
label: sweet potato row

planting.note: one 8 ft row, slips 12–15 in apart; vines will spill over the bed

bed30.note: one row down the middle on black plastic, slips 9–12 in apart; vines overrun the path by August — expected

watch_for: voles (UNH: can eat an entire harvest), deer browsing the vines, scurf (harmless black skin patches), wireworms in ground that was recently sod
watering: Water slips in well at planting; after that, little — overwatering fattens vines at the expense of roots.
method_notes: Honest marginality in zone 5b: it works but only just. Needs 90–120 frost-free days AND warm soil — UNH's data put soil under black plastic at 65°F by June 1 in Durham; plant slips only once soil is above 65°F and use black plastic to buy weeks. Start slips from storage roots 6–8 weeks out, or order them; choose early UNH-tested varieties (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Covington). Dig as late as possible but before hard frost (light frost on vines is fine); cure at 80–85°F, high humidity, 4–7 days. A cool, wet summer cuts yields hard — the most weather-dependent crop in this plan.
source: UNH Cooperative Extension Fact Sheet 'Growing Sweetpotatoes in New Hampshire' (Sideman — 90–120 frost-free days, soil >65°F, 9–12 in spacing, black plastic, pests, curing); UNH NH Agricultural Experiment Station cultivar trials (Beauregard, Covington highest yields; MOFGA Pest Report 2013 summary); MOFGA sweet potato feature (Maine growers, first-week-of-June planting, 1 ft slips, harvest late Sept); UMaine Maine Home Garden News Oct 2025 (harvest & curing).
